newsitem.title: USA: Race case lawyers step up campaign against Shell.
newsitem.headline: Race case lawyers step up campaign against Shell.

text.p: Lawyers representing plaintiffs in a long-running race discrimination case against Shell Oil Co on Wednesday stepped up their campaign against the company.

The Los Angeles-based law firm Hancock Rothert and Bunshoft, which is bringing a class action suit against Shell on behalf of 15 African American employees, said the Justice Department is looking at the possible implications of the merger between U.S. refining and marketing operations of Shell and Texaco Inc.

"The civil rights division of the Justice Department has never taken jurisdiction in a case like this but they have indicated to us that they are looking into whether or not they are going to exercise any jurisdiction," said Dominique Shelton of Hancock Rothert and Bunshoft.
The Justice Department said the matter is not currently before it, though it didn't rule out future action.

The law firm pointed out to the Justice Department that the merger agreement, announced last month, would give Texaco 44 percent of the new entity and Shell 56 percent. And the diversity program set up by Texaco last year as part of the settlement of its widely-publicized race discrimination case last year, only applies to subsidiaries in which Texaco has a stake of more than 50 percent, Shelton said.
"I think you'll see a number of civil rights organizations, once they realize the implications, asking for specific actions by Justice," said Shelton.
Though highlighting the Texaco employees, Shelton said the main concern of her firm is to underline that "what you have at Shell is one of the worst practices in terms of diversity."
The class action cases against Shell, first brought in 1995 in California and 1996 in Texas, are scheduled to come to trial in early September, 1997.

Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson, recently opening a Wall Street office for his Rainbow Coalition, specifically mentioned Shell's diversity record when saying oil companies would be among the main groups targeted.
Texaco and Shell note that the companies have specifically committed to a diversity program for the new joint company.
"It is too soon to outline any specific numbers or policies beyond saying that both companies have said they are committed to a 'model diversity program'," said Chris Gidez, a spokesman for Texaco.

"Throughout the discussions between the two companies, there has been a clear understanding that as the new company forms its own diversity plan, it will aspire to be a leader by embracing inclusion, openness and equal opportunity for all partners," Shell said in a statement.
"Shell is currently involved in settlement discussions with the plaintiffs in the discrimination lawsuits," the statement added.
